Three things we do not do today — and where they go

Woods stage 0 · Engage

The engage checklist

  • Stop. No valve, no controller, not yet.
  • Breathe. Name the emotion; naming drains it.
  • Assemble. Who must be here? Who has the history?
  • Declare the method. Name the framework out loud.
  • Do not guess. A named guess becomes a fact in ten minutes. อย่าเดา — ข้อสันนิษฐานกลายเป็นข้อเท็จจริงในสิบนาที

2-1 (b) · WHAT PRESSURE DOES TO YOU

Pressure does not make you stupid — it makes you narrow, then it anchors you

Now what pressure does to you.

Under pressure you…What it costs youThe written cure
Act before you understandThe evidence is gone before you lookSymptoms with times, before any valve moves
Narrow your attention(การตีบแคบของความสนใจ)Edge instruments go unscanned — the second symptom hides thereA scan checklist, every round

2-1 (d) · INTERACTIVE 2

Anchoring is only cheap when your first guess is genuinely likely

12 possible causes · one test = 1.5 h and 400 US dollars (USD) · downtime 600/h

Narrowing costs you the clue; the anchor costs you the hours — anchoring is paid in tests run down the wrong branch

2-1 (e) · THE ENGAGE CHECKLIST, WORKED

Three questions you answer before you say anything to anyone

None is about the plant — all three decide how good your next data is.

What am I afraid of?

Of being the engineer who let the heater trip. That fear says “more fuel” — the trend already shows more fuel buying less heat.

Who expects what, by when?

The operator wants T‑40 back at 355 °C this shift; the manager wants a cause by 08:00. Two clocks — so fix the cadence now: a call every 60 minutes, even with nothing new.

How much authority do I have?

Putting TC-30 in manual is yours. Cutting FC-3 feed — the change that started this — is not; that is the supervisor’s call.

2-2 · OUTLINE

Four questions, one order, one habit

2-2 (a) · THE FRAME

Marlin’s Four W’s — the whole first data set, in four questions

WHAT

The complaint, as a number: T‑40 = 341°C, normal 358

WHERE

Which point shows it — FC‑3 normal, deviation at T‑40

WHEN

Clock time and shape: step = switched · ramp = building · cyclic = a loop · spike = once

WHO

Who saw it, who acted — ask what they did, not what failed

FC = flow controller · TC = temperature controller · T‑40 = heater outlet. — Marlin drops Why and How: cause (สาเหตุ) is Week 4.

Cheapest and least disturbable source first

Questions are not equal, and neither are sources — each step aims the next one.

3FieldCosts legwork; aim it before you walk
4P&IDSlow; only once you know the line
Field first only if a leak, fire or trip is possible.

SECTION SUMMARY

First data: four questions, one order, one 72-hour rule

  • Four W’s: What (a number + its reference), Where (a pin on the flowsheet), When (clock time + shape), Who (observers/actors)
  • The trend’s shape names the family of causes: step = something was switched, ramp = accumulating, cyclic = a loop, spike = a single event
  • Order: historian → operator → the field → documents. Safety overrides the order.
  • Always ask: what changed in the last 72 hours?

Lecture 2-3 · Stage 1 Recognise

How do you know a problem has started, and from which data?

Detecting the signal, confirming it is real, and fixing the trigger that says “act now” เป้าหมาย: ตรวจจับสัญญาณบ่งชี้ความผิดปกติ และยืนยันว่ามีปัญหาเกิดขึ้นจริง

2-3 · OUTLINE

From a raw signal to a problem you can prove

  • Signals, sources and triggersWhat counts, where it is recorded, when to act
  • Delta plotsSeeing a fault the raw trend hides
  • Correlation and its trapsHow much two variables moving together prove
  • Many variables at onceWhat a pair of tags shows that one tag hides
  • Rate = coefficient × driving forceWhich part of the unit actually broke

1 · SIGNAL · SOURCE · TRIGGER

What says something is wrong, where it is written down, when it counts

Recognition starts before any theory: something must first say the plant has changed.

Signal

Process variable, product quality, equipment, safety, economics — or an operator’s ear.

Source

Historian, operator and maintenance logs, laboratory, accounting — plus interviews, field observation, plant tests.

Trigger

Outside spec, outside control limits, a pattern chance would not draw, or a new mean.

Spec limits come from the customer; control limits (UCL, LCL at \(\bar{x}\pm3\sigma\)) from the process.

INTERACTIVE — DRAG THE SLIDERS

Delta = actual − theoretical — the plot that sees what a raw trend hides

day the trigger is crossed
visible in the raw trend?
The theoretical value already carries feed rate and ambient conditions, so a delta removes deliberate load changes. Plot 6–10 essential variables this way daily: raise the throughput swing and the raw trace buries the fouling, yet the delta still crosses the trigger on the same day.

INTERACTIVE — 3 · CORRELATIONS

A scatter plot is simple, powerful, and easy to over-read

Agitation power against agitation rate: drag \(n\) down to a dozen and noise alone draws a convincing line — and data taken between 95 and 105 % of design says nothing about behaviour at 70 %.

4 · MULTIVARIATE ANALYSIS

Many variables at once — and what PCA finds

The explorer moved two variables. A real unit moves forty at once.

right: PC1 is the direction of most variation, PC2 the perpendicular one

PCA tells you where to look. It never tells you why.

4 · MULTIVARIATE ANALYSIS

Two tags, 250 batches — would you raise a flag?

One variable at a time is how a control room looks at an agitator: rate on one trend, power on another.

Inside limits, no trigger crossed — nothing here asks for your attention.

4 · MULTIVARIATE ANALYSIS

Plot one against the other, and the drift walks out

Same 250 batches. Nothing added — only rate plotted against power, coloured by time block.

Each marker style is a later block of batches. The last sits right and below the rest: the same rate now costs more power — a fouling or wearing agitator.

THE ENGINEERING SHORTCUT

One equation covers most unit operations

The charts say that something moved. This says which part of the equipment moved.

\[R \;=\; C \times DF\]

R = rate  ·  C = a lumped empirical coefficient  ·  DF = the theoretically correct driving force

Process\(R\)\(C\)\(DF\)
Heat transfer\(Q\)\(UA\)\(\Delta T_{lm}\)
Mass transfer\(N_A\)\(K_G a\,V\)\(\Delta p_A\)
Reaction\(-r_A\)\(k\)\(f(C_A)\)
Plot \(R\), \(C\) and \(DF\) separately in time. Whichever moved is the one that broke.

Recognise — what to carry out of 2-3

1

Recognition is a data activity: six kinds of signal, eight sources, one decision rule.

2

2-4

Lecture 2-4 · Set the trigger point

What should be a trigger variable, and where do you put the limit?

Choosing what to watch, and fixing the number that says “act now” เลือกตัวแปรที่จะเฝ้าระวัง และตั้งค่าเกณฑ์แจ้งเตือนให้มีที่มา

2-4 · Outline

From “which variable” to a defensible number

  • Criticality → multiplierWhy one variable earns 1σ and another 3σ
  • Four kinds of limitWho owns each one, and what crossing it means
  • PatternsThe signals that arrive before a limit is broken
  • No historyWhere the first \(\sigma\) comes from on a new unit

2-4 (a) · How tight is tight enough

Criticality ranking sets the multiplier

A trigger is defensible only when the number matches the consequence of missing it.
CriticalityTriggerReasoning
Critical1σCatch it early; false alarms cost less than the consequence
Medium2σBalanced — the usual industrial default
Low3σRespond only when it is unmistakable
Rank criticality first — by failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), or by Pareto.

2-4 (b) · Vocabulary confused daily

Four limits, four different owners

The ranking says which variable. Now: which of four limits is the trigger even on?
LimitSet byAnswersCrossing it means
Specification limitCustomer or contractIs the product saleable?Product is off-spec
Control limit (UCL / LCL)The process, from its \(\sigma\)Has the process changed?Investigate a special cause
Alarm limitOperationsMust the operator act?Operator response required
Trip limitThe safety studyIs it unsafe?Automatic shutdown

UCL and LCL = upper and lower control limit, computed as \(\bar{x} \pm k\sigma\)

2-4 (c) · Interactive — pick a pattern

Which rule fires, and what it means

A trend and a cycle can both stay inside 3σ: waiting for one point to break the limit means missing the two patterns that arrive earliest.

2-4 (d) · When you have no history

Estimating \(\sigma\) before the plant has a record

Every rule so far assumed \(\sigma\) was known. A new unit has none.

1 · A similar process

Compute \(\sigma\) from a comparable unit, product or campaign.

State why it is comparable.

2 · Design tolerance

Tolerance ±5 %? Then \(\sigma \approx \dfrac{\text{tolerance range}}{6}\)

Available before startup.

Write the basis and a review date beside the trigger. Triggers set too tight on a new unit teach operators to ignore alarms.

Section summary

Trigger points — what to carry out of 2-4

1

Rank criticality first, then choose 1σ, 2σ or 3σ to match.

2

Specification, control, alarm and trip limits have different owners and different meanings.

3

A tighter trigger buys earlier detection and pays in false alarms — a management choice.

2-5

Lecture 2-5 · Verify the problem is real

Is it a real problem — or is it just noise?

Confirming the deviation exists, and that it is worth resourcesยืนยันว่าปัญหาเป็นของจริง ไม่ใช่ noise และสำคัญพอที่จะใช้ทรัพยากรแก้

2-5 · Outline

Two questions, and the evidence each one needs

  • Three verification actionsValidate the data, confirm the trend, assess the impact
  • Cross-checking the readingWhat each check proves — and what it cannot
  • Noise or signalWhen variation earns investigation, and when it earns nothing
  • Instrument or processWhich reading to distrust first when two disagree

2-5 (a) · What you actually do

Three verification actions

Two tests: does the deviation exist, and is it worth resources?

1 · Validate the data

Check calibration; compare with a manual reading or a second sensor.

2 · Confirm the trend

Repeating, drifting, or once? Use the control-chart rules from 2-4.

3 · Assess the impact

Quantify safety, quality and cost per day — that sets urgency.

2-5 (b) · What the evidence is worth

What each check proves — and what it cannot

Action 1 is where most “process problems” quietly end.
CheckProvesCannot prove
Second element, same wellWhether one instrument is lyingAnything, if both share the fault
Laboratory re-analysisThat the result is repeatableThat the sample was representative
Mass / energy balanceWhether flows are mutually consistentWhich of the flows is wrong
Control-chart rulesThat variation is not randomThe cause of that variation

2-5 (c) · Interactive — drag the sliders

How big must a change be before you believe it?

Noise is common cause: correcting it only adds variation.การแก้ noise ทำให้กระบวนการแย่ลง ไม่ใช่ดีขึ้น
A change is believable only when it is large against the noise, or held long enough to be seen.

2-5 (d) · Interactive — cross-check the sensors

Is the instrument wrong, or the process?

T-40 and T-41 share one thermowell; the reactor outlet is a separate, downstream reading.
T-40 (°C)
T-41 same well (°C)
reactor outlet (°C)
Two agreeing elements prove nothing on their own: only the downstream reading separates a well fault from a real change.

Lecture 2-6 · Stage 2 Define

Which of these numbers can I actually trust?

Fact vs opinion, and checking how trustworthy the data is — this is the “home” of the idea

2-6 · OUTLINE

From a raw reading to a number you can build a definition on

  1. Fact, inference, opinionSort the three layers in one second, then drill it on a real log
  2. What an instrument really reportsA process value is a conversion, not a measurement
  3. Four standard liesfroth, density, immersion, range — worked once, then a virtual lab
  4. Does the balance close?The check that catches a meter nobody suspects

2-6 (a) · FACT / INFERENCE / OPINION

Three layers, and the one-second test for each

Stage 2 tells you to write down what you know — first you must know what is really known

  • Fact — could I have photographed it? A gauge reading, a valve position, a log entry
  • Inference (การอนุมาน) — does it need a because? Always revisable, so write it in another colour
  • Opinion — does it name a person? It never enters the problem statement
The middle layer hurts: an inference retold at handover until nobody rechecks it

2-6 (b) · INTERACTIVE 7

Classify each one. Fact, inference, or opinion?

Sorting the layers is a skill you drill, not a definition you memorise — try it on a real log

2-6 (c) · HOW AN INSTRUMENT LIES

An instrument reports its own variable: this one reports a pressure drop

\[\dot m = K\sqrt{\rho\,\Delta p}\]
\(\dot m\)
Mass flow reported
kg/s
\(K\)
Constant, set at commissioning
—
\(\rho\)
Density assumed in the conversion
kg/m³
\(\Delta p\)
Pressure drop — the only measured value
Pa
\[\frac{\dot m_{\text{true}}}{\dot m_{\text{ind}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\rho_{\text{actual}}}{\rho_{\text{design}}}}\]
  • Only \(\Delta p\) is measured; \(\rho\) was typed in at commissioning
  • Density 20 % wrong → flow 10 % wrong: too small to spot, enough to break the balance

Lecture 2-7 · Stage 2 Define

Where is the problem not — and why is that more powerful?

Bounding the problem with the IS / IS NOT technique (Bounding the Problem Space)

2-7 · OUTLINE

Four topics, and what each one settles

  • The 4 × 2 tableWhere each fact from 2-6 goes
  • Why the IS NOT column cutsIS describes; IS NOT kills causes
  • Tonight’s furnace and its twinA near-identical unit that is fine cuts deepest
  • Two clicks on the boundaryKill candidates, then place eight facts yourself

2-7 (a) · THE TOOL

Four dimensions cross two columns — and the right-hand one is the valuable one

2-6 gave us facts we can trust. Now we ask where they did not happen.

IS — it shows up hereIS NOT — it could have, and did not
WHATWhich variable deviates, by how muchWhich related variables stay on target
WHEREWhich unit, line, side, trainWhich comparable unit is still fine
WHENWhen it started, on which shiftThe periods it never occurs
EXTENTHow much, how far it spreadWhat has not spread

“Not on Mars” is no boundary (ขอบเขตปัญหา).

2-7 (b) · THE LOGIC

Confirmation adds weight. Contradiction removes candidates.

The table is filled in. Why is the right column worth more?

  • An IS fact fits many causes at once, so it eliminates nothing
  • An IS NOT fact is a contradiction test: any cause that predicts the problem there too is eliminated (ตัดออกถาวร), not merely weakened

SECTION SUMMARY

The boundary is the cheapest analysis you will ever do

  • 4 × 2: What / Where / When / Extent crossed with IS and IS NOT
  • IS NOT eliminates; IS only describes. A usable IS NOT names what could have been hit and was not
  • Find the twin. Everything two comparable units share is eliminated in one line
  • Every IS NOT becomes a constraint that a Week 4 hypothesis has to pass

2-8 (a) · THE SENTENCE

Five slots, five facts — if you cannot fill one, you are not ready to write

[measured variable] at [location] moved from [normal value] to [current value] since [time], while [what is still normal] did not

One fact per slot: the deviation, the boundary and the timing Week 4 needs

Furnace outlet temperature T‑40 at H‑201 train A fell from 358°C to 341°C and still falling at 0.4°C/min since 01:34 while feed flow, unit pressure, drum level and all of train B are still normal

SECTION SUMMARY

One sentence, five slots — line 1 of your Trouble-Shooter’s Worksheet

  • Template: variable at location, from normal value to current value, since a stated time, while named things stay normal
  • Three defects: a buried cause, an unmeasurable word, an opinion about people

A target you can be judged against

  • SMARTS-$: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Reliable, Timely, Safely, Cost-effective

Case Study · Woods Case 27 — the IPA column

Where is the IPA going — and what does each answer cost?

Stages 0, 1 and 2 of a real diagnosis, priced at $4,000 an hour of lost production

CASE STUDY · THE PLAN

One case, four stages, one price list

  1. Stage 0 — the problemThe plant, the complaint, and the one number: 0.70
  2. Stage 1 — EngageHazard data decides: stop the plant, or keep running?
  3. Stage 2 — DefineFive cheap actions buy one testable problem statement
  4. The action menuAll 69 actions, priced as lost production at $4,000 an hour

STAGE 0 · THE PLANT

An IPA column with a brand-new air-cooled condenser

STAGE 0 · THE COMPLAINT AND THE NUMBER

0.995 became 0.70 — where is the IPA going?

“Recently, the water-cooled condenser on the IPA column was replaced by an air-cooled condenser… Since the installation, the ratio of IPA out to IPA fed to the column is 0.70. Previously we could account for 0.995. Where is the IPA going? This costs us $4,000/h.”
Plant balance, bought later as action 1508: of every 2250 kg fed, 675 kg is unaccounted for. Nothing here yet says why.

STAGE 0 · HOW THIS CASE IS PRICED

In this case the price list is a clock

Every action in this case is priced at the production it destroys while you wait for the answer — elapsed time × $4,000/h. Nothing else.

Check it yourself: action 1916 is “run cold water over the tubes for an 8-hour shift” and it is priced at $32,000. 8 h × $4,000/h = $32,000, exactly.

So “how much did your diagnosis cost?” and “how long did you take?” are the same question. Buying all 69 actions = 70.5 hours = $282,100.
PriceTime it stands forTypical action
$650≈ 10 mina phone call, a file
$1,20018 minread a control-room trend
$3,20048 mina field survey
$8,0002 hcalibrate a sensor
$10,0002.5 ha set of lab samples
$20,0005 hopen and inspect
$32,0008 hone shift of plant trial

STAGE 0 · YOUR TURN

You have a complaint and one number. What do you buy?

The plant is losing $4,000 an hour. Every button below spends some of that hour.

Spent$0
Production lost0.00 h
Woods bought0 / 0
Pick an actionEvery action is priced in lost production — $4,000 for each hour it takes.

Woods spends $0 at Stage 0. Nothing here is bought; the complaint is only sorted into fact, inference and opinion.

Stage 0 has one job — sorting what you were told — and it is free.

STAGE 0 · DISCIPLINE

Sort what you were told before you use it

StatementStatusWhy it matters
“The ratio out/in is 0.70”FACTA measured plant balance. Everything else must explain this number.
“Since the installation”FACTA change problem. Find the change and you usually find the cause.
“Where is the IPA going?”INFERENCEIt assumes the IPA leaves the plant. It might instead never have been made, or be mis-measured.
“The new condenser must be too small”OPINIONThe most popular first guess in this case — and the design file kills it for $1,000.
“It is a hot day, so the fans can’t cope”OPINIONPlausible, testable, and — as we will see — wrong. Test it cheaply, not expensively.
The two facts are free. The two opinions cost money to settle. Spend on the cheapest test that can kill an opinion, never on the one that merely confirms it.

STAGE 1 · YOUR TURN

Engage: is this an emergency, and what do you read first?

Engage decides urgency before diagnosis. Three of these stop the plant; one reads it.

Spent$0
Production lost0.00 h
Woods bought0 / 0
Pick an actionThe four safety actions all cost $650. What differs is what they do to the plant.

Woods buys 2529 only — $650, 10 minutes. IPA is NFPA 1, 3, 0: a flammable liquid, not an acute toxic release.

Ten minutes of hazard data buys the right to keep running.

STAGE 1 · HAZARD FIRST

Read the hazard data, then decline the shutdown

2529 — $650
IPA is NFPA 1, 3, 0.
  • Health 1 — irritation only, no toxic emergency.
  • Flammability 3 — the real hazard, and why the flare matters.
  • Reactivity 0 — stable; nothing is running away.
  • The losses go to a designed vent scrubber and flare, inside the process.
The three ways to stop the plantVerdict
1 · safe-park the unit“Not needed.” $650
271 · interlock shutdown“Not needed.” $650
122 · SIS plus evacuation“Not needed.” $650
Expensive is not the same as dangerous. Nothing is over-pressured or over-temperature, so the right answer is to keep running and investigate fast — and the MSDS is what lets you defend that.

STAGE 1.3 · THE HINGE

Name the one principle this diagnosis will hinge on

The deviation is a mass balance, not a temperature. So the fundamental that decides this case is where vapour can go, not how much heat the bundle can move.
  • If the condenser were merely undersized, the exit liquid would run hot and the receiver pressure would climb. Neither is reported.
  • If the seal is lost, vapour bypasses the tubes entirely and the exit liquid still reads perfectly normal — because what does condense condenses properly.
  • That distinction — rate versus route — is the whole case.
\(\dot m_{\text{IPA,in}} = \dot m_{\text{bottoms}} + \dot m_{\text{product}} + \underbrace{\dot m_{\text{slip}}}_{?}\)
Everything from here on is an attempt to give the last term a name. Woods’ colleagues will offer nine candidate names in Stage 3.

STAGE 2 · YOUR TURN

Define: which five actions buy you the problem statement?

You know it is not an emergency. Now spend on understanding, not on hardware.

Spent$0
Production lost0.00 h
Woods bought0 / 0
Pick an actionFive of these eight are what Define is made of. Three are hardware bought too early.

Woods spends $6,800 · 1.7 h in Define: 2134, 398, 1758, 1259 ($2,600) then 1508 ($4,200). The whole case closes at $23,450.

$2,600 of cheap questions plus one $4,200 number write the whole statement.

STAGE 2.1–2.2 · THE SKETCH

Action 2134 ($650) tells you how the unit is really piped

“… The overhead line from the top of the column goes vertically down and then across to the feed header of the condenser. The exit from the liquid header containing the condensed IPA goes directly to the overhead receiver. From the overhead receiver the condensed IPA is pumped to downstream units. Any uncondensed inerts from the overhead receiver go to the vent scrubber system.”

STAGE 2.3 · CLOSE THE BALANCE

Turn the ratio into kilograms per second

StreamFlowIPAIPA flow
Feed · 23942.78 kg/s50 % w/w1.39 kg/s
Bottoms · 2846, 16581.38 kg/s10 % w/w0.138 kg/s
Overhead product——0.834 kg/s
Unaccounted——0.418 kg/s
Cross-check: action 1508 gives 2250 kg in, 1575 kg out over the same period — 1575/2250 = 0.700. The instantaneous flows and the integrated balance agree.
\(\dot m_{\text{slip}} = 1.39 - 0.138 - 0.834 = 0.418\ \mathrm{kg/s}\)
1500 kg of IPA per hour is leaving as vapour. At the stated $4,000/h that values IPA at about $2.7/kg — the plant’s own arithmetic is self-consistent.
Note what this rules out already: the bottoms carry only 0.138 kg/s of IPA in total. Even if all of it were an error, it could not explain a 0.418 kg/s hole.

STAGE 2.4–2.5 · BOUND THE PROBLEM

Only two things deviate — and four questions say where

VariableCurrentShould be
IPA accounted for0.700.995
Vent scrubber load · 1291pulsingsteady, small
Temperatures, pressures, levelsas expectedno deviation
Everything the control room shows is normal — a clue, not a dead end: the fault is intermittent.
 ISIS NOT
What · 398The balance does not close on IPANothing else changed
When · 1758Since the new installationNever before it
Where · 1708Here and downstreamNot upstream
Who · 1002Our operators, downstream plantVent scrubber people — not asked yet
“Since the installation” makes this a change problem: the cause is inside what was changed.

STAGE 2.6–2.7 · CHANGES, GOAL, GAPS

What changed? Almost nothing — which is the point

1259 · $650
“Changes only made to the condenser and associated piping.”
It does not say “the condenser”. It says the condenser and its pipework — that is the suspect list.
447 · $650 — hot, 35 °C, 80 % RH. The weather is a trap; Stage 3 kills it for $3,200.
Goal · 2162 · $650
“To prevent the apparent loss of IPA.” Woods’ careful word: a measurement error is still on the table.

Still missing — this drives Stage 3

  • Vapour, liquid, or never leaving at all?
  • Continuous, or in pulses?
  • Can the condenser cope on a hot day?

STAGE 2 · THE DELIVERABLE

The problem statement — one sentence, quotable, testable

Since the air-cooled condenser and its associated piping were installed at the last turnaround, 0.418 kg/s of IPA — 30 % of the feed — leaves the overhead system without being condensed, in pulses, while every control-room variable reads normal; at a cost of $4,000/h.

It names the boundary

“The overhead system” — not the column, not the feed.

It names the quantity

0.418 kg/s. Any hypothesis must explain a hole this big, not a small one.

It names the signature

“In pulses, while everything reads normal.” That sentence alone eliminates most of the nine hypotheses.
